title: Cheap on average
objectives: Explain amortised cost with a list that grows by doubling.

screens.title: Where does the next tick go?
screens.prose:
A growable array keeps spare slots. It starts with capacity 1. When it is full, it allocates a block twice as big and copies every element across.

```python
if size == capacity:          # full
    capacity = 2 * capacity   # new block, twice as big
    # copy all `size` elements across
slots[size] = x
size += 1
```

Step through the appends. Dashed slots are not allocated yet; green cells were just copied.
screens.question: How many elements did the 9th append copy?

widget.label: Copies made by the 9th append
widget.accept: 8: the array was full at 8, so all 8 moved to a block of 16.

hints.text: Step from 8 appends to 9 and watch the capacity.
At 8 appends every slot is full.
The 9th append finds 8 full slots, allocates 16 and copies the 8 old elements.

feedback.correct: Eight copies: the whole array moved.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the caption as you step from 8 appends to 9.

byKey.write: You counted writing the new tick. The 9th append also moved the 8 old elements to the new block.
byKey.plus-new: You counted the new tick as a copy. It is written once, not copied; the 8 old elements are copied.
byKey.total: That is the total over all 9 appends. The question asks about the 9th alone.

explain.text: Most appends just fill a spare slot. An append that finds the array full copies everything: 1, then 2, then 4, then 8 elements. Python's `list.append` works this way, with a much smaller growth factor of about 1.125.

screens.title: Add up the copies
screens.prose: The bars show the copies each append makes, for 16 appends from capacity 1. The spikes come when the array is full at size 1, 2, 4 and 8.
screens.question: Fill in the total copies after $n$ appends.

hints.text: Add the bars from append 1 up to append $n$.
Append 1 fills the one starting slot, so it copies nothing.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the bars up to and including append $n$.

byKey.r0c1: The first append fills the starting slot of capacity 1. Nothing is copied.
byKey.r4c1: For 16 appends, add the spikes at appends 2, 3, 5 and 9: $1 + 2 + 4 + 8$.
byKey.r2c1: For 4 appends, the spikes are at appends 2 and 3: $1 + 2$.

explain.text: Each total is $1 + 2 + 4 + \dots$, a geometric sum, and it comes to $n - 1$ when $n$ is a power of two. The edge case $n = 1$ costs nothing, because the starting slot is free.

screens.title: Copies per append
screens.prose: Some appends are expensive and most are free. Spread the copying evenly over all the appends.
screens.question: On average, how many copies does each of the 16 appends make?

hints.text: Average means total divided by the number of appends.
The total for 16 appends is 15.

feedback.correct: Under one copy per append, on average.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the total copies by 16.

byKey.worst: That is the worst single append. The average spreads its cost over all 16.
byKey.total: That is the total. Divide it by the 16 appends.
byKey.spikes: You averaged over the 4 expensive appends only. The cheap ones count too.

explain.text: Fifteen copies spread over 16 appends is under one copy each. This average over a whole sequence of operations is the **amortised** cost. Each append is amortised $O(1)$, though a few cost much more.

screens.title: One bad append
screens.prose: Over 1,000 appends, the bars show only the appends that resize. Append 513 copies 512 elements. A colleague concludes that appending is $O(n)$.
screens.question: What is the average number of copies per append over all 1,000 appends?

hints.text: Add every bar, then divide by all 1,000 appends.
The bars are $1, 2, 4, \dots, 512$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Total the bars, then divide by 1,000, not by 10.

byKey.worst: You took the worst single append as the typical one. Only 10 of the 1,000 appends copy anything.
byKey.total: That is the total. Spread it over the 1,000 appends.
byKey.tenth: You divided by the 10 resizes. The other 990 appends copy nothing and count too.

explain.text: The total is $1 + 2 + \dots + 512 = 1{,}023$, about one copy per append. The worst single append is $O(n)$, but it is rare: the next one is twice as far away. So a run of $n$ appends costs $O(n)$ in all.

screens.title: Why the total stays below $2n$
screens.prose: We bound the total copies for $n$ appends with the doubling policy. Put the argument in order.
screens.question: Put the lines of the argument in order.

lines.text: Copies happen only when the array is full at size $1, 2, 4, \dots, 2^{m-1}$, with $2^{m-1} < n$.
Since $2^{m-1} < n$, we have $2^m < 2n$, so the total is below $2n$.
Dividing by $n$: fewer than 2 copies per append, which is amortised $O(1)$.

hints.text: Start from when a copy happens at all.
The geometric sum formula from the series course turns the sum into $2^m - 1$.
When copies happen, the sum they make, its closed form, the bound $2n$, then per append.

feedback.correct: Total under $2n$, so under 2 copies per append.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each line uses the one before it.

byKey.amort: The per-append claim needs the total bound first.
byKey.geo: You need the sum written out before you can close it.

explain.text: The copies form $1 + 2 + \dots + 2^{m-1} = 2^m - 1$, and the largest term is below $n$. So the total is under $2n$. For 1,000 appends: $1{,}023 < 2{,}000$.

screens.prose:
With doubling, $n$ appends make

$$1 + 2 + 4 + \dots + 2^{m-1} = 2^m - 1 < 2n$$

copies in total. That is $O(n)$ for the whole run, and **amortised** $O(1)$ per append. One append can still cost $O(n)$, but those appends get rarer as the array grows.
screens.question: The policy changes to tripling the capacity when full. What is the amortised cost of an append?

options.why: You took the worst append as the average. Tripling gives copies $1 + 3 + 9 + \dots$, a geometric sum below $\tfrac{3n}{2}$.
There are about $\log_3 n$ resizes, but their copies add to a geometric sum below a constant times $n$.

options.text: $O(1)$ but more total copies than doubling
options.why: Not in general: tripling's total stays under $1.5n$, against $2n$ for doubling. The price is more spare slots.

feedback.correct: Any constant growth factor above 1 gives amortised $O(1)$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write out the copies as a sum and bound it.

explain.text: Tripling gives copies $1 + 3 + 9 + \dots$, still a geometric sum dominated by its last term, which is below $n$. The total is under $1.5n$, so appends stay amortised $O(1)$. The price is more unused slots.

screens.title: Simulate the array
screens.prose: The policy, exactly: capacity starts at 1 and size at 0. Before writing an element, if `size == capacity`, double the capacity and count `size` copies. Writing the new element is not a copy.

state.caption: After 5 appends: capacity 8, 7 copies in all

screens.question: Write `total_copies(n)`: the total number of element copies made by $n$ appends.

widget.how: Check runs 10 hidden tests, for $n$ from 0 to 1,025. They include $n = 1$ (no copy) and the step from 1,024 to 1,025.

hints.text: Loop `n` times; each time round is one append.
Check for a full array before you write, not after.
In the loop: `if size == capacity: capacity *= 2; copies += size`, then `size += 1`. Return `copies`.

feedback.correct: Your counts match $2^m - 1$ at every size.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-2: Test 2 expects 0 for one append: the starting slot holds it. If you got 1, you resized before checking for space.
byKey.test-3: Test 3 expects 1 for two appends. Count the elements already stored, not the new one.
byKey.test-10: Test 10 expects 2,047: append 1,025 finds 1,024 full slots and copies all of them.

explain.text: Your simulation reproduces the table: 15 copies for 16 appends, 1,023 for 1,000. The jump from 1,023 to 2,047 at $n = 1{,}025$ is one expensive append. Divided over all appends, it is still under 2 each.

screens.title: Growing by ten
screens.prose: Another policy starts at capacity 10 and adds 10 slots each time the array fills. Each resize is small, so it sounds thrifty.
screens.question: How many copies do 1,000 appends make under this policy?

hints.text: The array is full at sizes 10, 20, 30, and so on. Each resize copies that many.
The last resize happens at append 991, copying 990.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the copies of every resize: $10, 20, \dots, 990$.

byKey.resizes: That is the number of resizes. Each one copies every element stored so far.
byKey.doubling: That is the doubling policy's total. Here the resizes are small but far more frequent.
byKey.ten-each: You counted 10 copies per resize. A resize copies all the elements, not just the last 10.
byKey.to-1000: The array is never full at 1,000 here: the last resize is at size 990.

explain.text: The copies are $10 + 20 + \dots + 990 = 49{,}500$, against 1,023 for doubling. In general about $\tfrac{n^2}{20}$: growing by a fixed amount makes $n$ appends $O(n^2)$. The resizes must get further apart, which doubling does.

canvas.caption: Copies grow by 10 per resize: an arithmetic sum, $O(n^2)$

screens.title: Taking from the front
screens.prose: A queue of ticks waits to be processed, oldest first. `ticks.pop(0)` removes the front of a Python list, and every element behind it shifts one slot left.
screens.question: Draining 1,000 ticks with `pop(0)` until the list is empty: how many element shifts in total?

hints.text: The first pop shifts the 999 ticks behind it.
Each pop leaves one fewer tick to shift.

feedback.correct: Half a million shifts: $O(n^2)$ to drain the queue.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the shifts of every pop.

byKey.n: You counted one step per pop. Each `pop(0)` shifts every remaining tick.
byKey.one-pop: That is the first pop alone. The next pops shift 998, 997, and so on.

explain.text: Each `pop(0)` is $O(n)$, so draining is $O(n^2)$: the pair sum from lesson 1. `collections.deque` keeps both ends free, so `popleft()` is $O(1)$ and draining is $O(n)$. The data structures course builds it.

screens.title: An order book's tick log
screens.prose: An order book appends every tick to a growable array with the doubling policy. On a busy day it receives 2,000,000 ticks.

state.caption: The last resize happens at tick 1,048,577, which is $2^{20} + 1$

screens.question: Over the whole day, how many copies per tick is that on average?

hints.text: Does any resize happen between tick 1,048,577 and tick 2,000,000?
The capacity after tick 1,048,577 is 2,097,152, more than 2,000,000.
No more resizes, so the total stays 2,097,151. Divide by 2,000,000: about 1.05.

feedback.correct: About one copy per tick, as the bound $2n$ promised.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the total copies, then divide by 2,000,000.

byKey.worst: That is the single worst append, at tick 1,048,577. Averaged over the day it is about one copy per tick.
byKey.half: You divided the copies of the last resize alone. The total is 2,097,151.

explain.text: No resize happens after tick 1,048,577, so the total is 2,097,151: about 1.05 copies per tick. One tick that day paid for a million copies, which is a latency spike to know about. A `numpy` array pre-allocated at the expected size avoids even that.

ideas: A doubling array copies $1 + 2 + 4 + \dots$ elements in all: a geometric sum below $2n$ for $n$ appends.
So appends are amortised $O(1)$: averaged over the run, though one append can copy $O(n)$ elements.
Growing by a fixed number of slots makes $n$ appends $O(n^2)$, and so does `pop(0)` from a list. A `deque` and pre-allocation avoid both.
summary.trap: The worst append is not the average: one append in 1,000 copied 512 elements, but the average was about 1.

quiz.prose:
```python
import numpy as np
out = np.array([])
for x in ticks:
    out = np.append(out, x)
```
`np.append` returns a new array holding a copy of `out` plus `x`.
quiz.question: For $n$ ticks, what is the total cost of this loop?

options.text: $O(n^2)$: every append copies the whole array

options.why: That holds for `list.append`, which keeps spare slots. `np.append` copies everything every time.
There is no doubling here: the calls copy $0, 1, 2, \dots$ elements, an arithmetic sum.
Vectorising helps whole-array operations. A Python loop of copies is still $0 + 1 + \dots + (n - 1)$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. How many elements does call number $k$ copy?

explain.text: Call $k$ copies $k - 1$ elements, so the total is $\tfrac{n(n-1)}{2}$. Pre-allocate with `np.empty(n)` and fill `out[i] = x`, or collect in a list and convert once.

quiz.prose: A growable array starts at capacity 1 and doubles when full. You make 100 appends.
quiz.question: How many copies does the most expensive of these appends make?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. At which size is the array last full before 100?

byKey.hundred: The array is never full at 99. It is full at 64, and next at 128.
byKey.total: That is the total over all 100 appends. The worst single append is one term of it.
byKey.next: The array would be full at 128, but 100 appends never get there.

explain.text: The array is full at sizes 1, 2, 4, ..., 64. Append 65 copies 64 elements into a block of 128, and no later append among the 100 resizes again.

quiz.prose: A strategy keeps the last 500 prices. Each new price is added at one end and the oldest dropped from the other.
quiz.question: Which structure keeps both operations $O(1)$?

options.why: `pop(0)` shifts all the remaining prices, so dropping the oldest is $O(n)$.
`insert(0, p)` shifts every price right, which is $O(n)$.
Finding the oldest key in a plain dict is not what it is built for. A deque does both ends directly.

feedback.correct: A deque is cheap at both ends.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which operations shift every element of a list?

explain.text: A Python list is cheap at its end only. `deque` is built for both ends, and `maxlen` drops the oldest price for you on each append.

quiz.prose: Same doubling policy, capacity starting at 1.
quiz.question: How many copies does a single append to the empty array make?

options.why: Writing the new element is not a copy. Nothing was stored before, so nothing moves.
The array has room for one element, so no resize happens.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Is the array full before the first append?

explain.text: Capacity 1 and size 0 means a free slot. The first append writes into it and copies nothing.
